video_title: I let the Internet Design A (Bad) Military - Orbital Strikes to Battleships, Arming Emutopia Special
gist: Perun runs a deliberately comedic procurement thought experiment - crowdsourced picks (M7 rifle, T-14 Armata, Queen Elizabeth carriers, an aviation battleship, XL-UUV 'submarine carriers', orbital tungsten rods, space marines) for the fictional state of Emutopia - and reverse-engineers plausible-sounding justifications for each. The serious payload is a procurement-economics lesson: requirement wording (not the tender itself) determines the winner, individually defensible buys can hollow out a force when summed, and opportunity cost plus creative reuse of existing platforms usually beats buying the shiny thing.

themes.theme: Requirement-Setting as the Real Selection Lever

insights.claim: Perun argues that procurement outcomes are usually predetermined by how the initial requirement is written rather than by bias or corruption inside the evaluation process itself, since a single line item on weight, armament or compatibility can eliminate most of the field before any design is scored.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: When assessing a defence tender's likely winner, read the requirements document, not the shortlist - incumbents and favoured suppliers are visible in the spec long before award.
insights.quote: I didn't have to specifically say, I want to rig the selection process in favor of the T-14 Armata. I just had to set much more reasonable-sounding parameters

insights.claim: Perun demonstrates that a 'risk reduction' clause requiring the selected system to already be in service with a major military, or to have seen combat, is a common-sense-sounding filter that in practice hands the competition to a predetermined incumbent regardless of the design's actual merit.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Combat-proven and in-service clauses are structural moats for established primes and a red flag that a tender is not genuinely open.
insights.quote: This reduces Imutopia's risk because no major military would ever purchase a dud

insights.claim: Perun frames the core requirements-writing tension as being prescriptive enough to steer industry without either writing out creative solutions or discovering at the end of a program that the stated requirement was not the actual need, citing the B-2's low-level bombing 'nice-to-have' as costing multiple years of delay and engineering sacrifices.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Program-risk screening should focus on the requirement/nice-to-have boundary - that is where schedule slips and cost growth are usually seeded.

insights.claim: Perun warns that individually defensible equipment purchases become incoherent when summed, because tunnel vision on single platforms without a force-level concept forces planners to backward-engineer a strategy around whatever capital equipment they bought.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Evaluate defence primes' order books at portfolio level - a national force plan that hollows the escort tier eventually forces a corrective buy cycle in the neglected segment.
insights.quote: It is entirely possible to put up a piece of equipment that by itself might come with a great sales pitch and an excellent stat sheet, and yet it not be the correct fit for the overall force.

insights.claim: Perun advocates a 'recycle before replace' logic check, noting that repurposing existing platforms is usually far more efficient than wholesale replacement because replacement drags in a new sustainment plan and training pipeline, and citing the Hawker Typhoon becoming a ground-attack aircraft and the Me 110 becoming a night fighter as historical precedent.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Upgrade and role-change programs are a persistently underrated revenue pool versus headline new-build platforms.
insights.quote: before you replace, it's decent to throw in a logic check to see if you can first recycle

insights.claim: Perun argues the decisive procurement and logistics consequence of moving from 5.56 NATO to a higher-pressure round like the M7's is simply that larger rounds are larger, forcing soldiers either to cut their ammunition load or carry more weight for the same round count.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Next-generation rifle programs carry a hidden logistics tax - magazine capacity, load-carriage and resupply volume - that rarely appears in the headline unit price.
insights.quote: it's that larger rounds are larger

insights.claim: Perun notes that abandoning 5.56 NATO forfeits ammunition cross-compatibility with a large number of allied forces plus access to massive global stockpiles and production capacity, an interoperability and surge-supply cost that a national cartridge change quietly imposes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cartridge changes fragment the allied ammunition base and create long-tail demand for new production lines rather than drawing on existing surplus.

insights.claim: Perun contends that Ukraine's experience argues against heavier infantry rifles because long dismounted movements make weight a premium, and long-range lethality against infantry there is delivered by FPV drones and artillery rather than small arms, so spare carrying capacity is better spent on drone batteries or a CQB shotgun.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Demand signal favours infantry drone kit and load-carriage over next-generation rifle programs; treat NGSW-style budgets as contestable.

insights.claim: Perun shows how a speculative future threat - armoured UGVs and robotic combatants, which he concedes do not currently exist in heavily armoured form - can be written into a requirement as a mandatory penetration threshold, letting a preferred cartridge win almost by default.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Watch for 'future-proofing' threat assumptions in requirements documents - they are the cheapest way to narrow a field without an explicit sole-source decision.
insights.quote: It doesn't matter that heavily armored robotic combatants don't necessarily exist now, they could.

themes.theme: Armoured Vehicle Economics and the High-Low Ground Mix

insights.claim: Perun highlights that Russia planned 2,300 T-14 Armatas by 2025 but produced only a handful, with hesitation predating the Ukraine war - then-Deputy PM Yuri Borisov said in 2018 that money would go to upgraded older designs instead.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A canonical case of a next-generation platform losing to upgrade economics - relevant to any next-gen ground vehicle program pitching a clean-sheet design.
insights.quote: Why flood our military with Armatas? The T-72s are in great demand in the markets.

insights.claim: Perun cites Borisov's justification that upgraded T-72s beat German, French and US MBTs on 'price, efficiency, and quality' and that with a military budget ten times smaller than NATO's Russia achieves objectives through such efficient solutions, framing cost-per-effect as an explicit Russian doctrinal choice rather than a fallback.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Budget-constrained buyers systematically favour upgrade packages over new platforms - a structural tailwind for retrofit and modernisation contractors.
insights.quote: 10 times smaller than that of NATO, we are achieving our objectives due to such efficient solutions.

insights.claim: Perun shows a weight cap justified by bridges, airlift or landing craft, plus an uncrewed-turret requirement, a minimum gun calibre, a hard-kill active protection system and drone-swatting remote weapon station, is enough to eliminate the Leopard 2A8, modernised Abrams and Challenger 3 while leaving the Armata technically compliant.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Weight limits and turret architecture clauses are the single most powerful discriminators in MBT tenders - track them in any upcoming armour competition.

insights.claim: Perun endorses a genuine high-low doctrinal mix in which technicals and cheap civilian-derived vehicles operate behind a small high-end armoured tier, arguing speed, mobility and attritability can matter more than raw protection and that flat-bed civilian vehicles can carry sensors, air-defence weapons, supplies or troops.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Rugged commercial vehicle demand is a real and scaling defence line item, not a curiosity.

insights.claim: Perun notes demand for rugged civilian vehicles on the Ukrainian battlefield became large enough that the Ukrainian MOD ran its own procurements for thousands of them to augment volunteer-supplied vehicles, and that Ukrainians have used technicals as guided-missile launch platforms and as anti-aircraft carriers in mobile fire groups hunting Shahed-style drones.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Confirms a durable, state-level procurement channel for commercial 4x4s and pickup conversions in high-intensity war.

insights.claim: Perun argues that mass corrugated-iron shelters - real shelters plus layered dummy shelters over aircraft, vehicles and stores - are an extremely cheap counter to satellite-based targeting because they impose an unfavourable cost exchange on an attacker's ballistic missile inventory.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Low-cost concealment and decoy infrastructure is an underpriced defensive investment relative to active missile defence.
insights.quote: they better be building billions in ballistic missiles to blow up a bunch of bulk buildings from Bunnings

insights.claim: Perun justifies buying roughly 100 Lamborghinis - only about 12 for actual reconnaissance - on the grounds that the real problem is recruitment and retention, arguing volunteer militaries must spend heavily on attracting and keeping personnel and that a few cruise missiles' worth of spending on a recruiting hook can be rational.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Personnel attraction and retention is a real, growing and often unbudgeted competitor for hardware dollars in all-volunteer forces.
insights.quote: the problem we're trying to solve here isn't actually reconnaissance, it's recruitment and retention

themes.theme: Capital Ships and the Hollowed-Out Middle Fleet

insights.claim: Perun identifies three binding constraints on a middle power buying two Queen Elizabeth class carriers - each over 280 m and 80,000 tons - namely shipyard and workforce capacity on a reasonable timeline, costs that would cannibalise other critical naval investment unless stretched over an unreasonable period, and oppressive crewing requirements.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Carrier ambitions for mid-tier navies are gated by yards and crews more than by sticker price - watch workforce and drydock capacity as the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Perun floats a multinational 'time-share' carrier fleet across the UK, Canada and Emutopia - a single procurement and maintenance plan for four hulls, deep maintenance in the UK, some servicing in the other two theatres - as a way to spread industrial and cost burden and enable one carrier permanently deployed with surge to two or three.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Joint multinational capital-ship ownership models would concentrate sustainment revenue in a single lead yard while breaking the one-nation-one-hull cost ceiling.

insights.claim: Perun points to the Soviet Kiev class heavy aviation cruiser - about 45,000 tons, flight deck for helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft, eight P-500 Sandbox launchers with roughly 550 km range plus reloads, and twelve on Baku without reloads - as showing a committee's 'battleship' specification is not entirely outside the realm of possibility.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Historical hybrid aviation-cruiser designs are the reference class for today's large multi-role combatant proposals.

insights.claim: Perun's modernised battleship concept swaps bulky crewed aircraft for drones such as Ghost Bats, replaces heavy anti-ship missiles with a large VLS field, and uses nuclear propulsion to power directed energy weapons that start as microwave and laser self-defence and might scale to fleet defence over time.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Nuclear propulsion as a power source for directed energy, plus drone-first air wings, is the plausible technical core of any future large-combatant pitch.

insights.claim: Perun exposes the standard Swiss Army knife funding trick: a multi-role ship is affordable only by cutting the specialised LHA/LHD, frigate, hospital ship and command ship that each did the job better, and concentrating capabilities in one hull removes the option of having them in different places at once.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Multi-mission consolidation pitches should be stress-tested against dispersion value - the offsets funding them usually destroy fleet flexibility.

insights.claim: Perun characterises the resulting fleet as top and bottom-heavy, with displacement and manpower concentrated in carriers and battleships and the remaining money in underwater drones, leaving minesweepers, patrol boats, corvettes, frigates and destroyers short-funded and every remaining escort tied to carrier protection.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Escort and mine-warfare shortfalls are the predictable second-order consequence of capital-ship-led naval plans - a recurring source of later emergency procurement.

insights.claim: Perun proposes turning extra-large UUVs such as Australia's Ghost Shark and America's Orca into 'submarine aircraft carriers' by fitting a payload module that launches FPVs or loitering munitions, arguing this is only an incremental ask given navies already treat XL-UUVs as multi-purpose payload carriers for sensors, robotic payloads and mines.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Payload-module ecosystems, not the hulls, are where XL-UUV value accrues - watch modular payload contracts around Ghost Shark and Orca.

insights.claim: Perun notes Ukraine has repeatedly launched FPVs from small surface drones, trading warhead size for reusability, extra range and precision against soft, valuable, hard-to-conceal coastal targets like radars and air defence installations.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The drone-carrier-drone pattern is now battle-proven and is the template for the next generation of uncrewed maritime strike.

insights.claim: Perun argues uncrewed submarines are far easier to surge in wartime than crewed submarines because you cannot rush-build trained and experienced crews, so designing XL-UUVs for wartime mass production - right tooling in advance, stockpiled long-lead items, maximum commercial off-the-shelf content - lets a country 'hit print' on a navy given warning of a crisis.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Warm-tooling and long-lead-item stockpiling is the concrete, fundable form of 'mobilisation readiness' - a distinct spending category from platform buys.

insights.claim: Perun frames a drone-heavy navy as explicitly optimised for deterrence by punishment rather than deterrence by denial, applying lessons from Ukraine, Iran and the Houthis with better technology and more scale to make civilian traffic into opposing ports prohibitively risky and pin down disproportionate ASW assets.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Punishment-based maritime deterrence favours cheap distributed effectors and mines over blue-water escorts - a spending mix shift for middle powers.
insights.quote: We don't try and go down the road of deterrence by denial. We don't have the resources for it. Instead, the name of the game is deterrence by punishment.

insights.claim: Perun concedes an uncrewed-heavy fleet buys wartime asymmetry at the cost of peacetime utility, since there is only so much disaster relief you can do with a robotic submarine - a navy optimised for punishment underperforms across the constabulary and humanitarian roles that dominate peacetime tasking.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Peacetime presence value is a real, often-decisive political constraint that argues against fully attritable fleet designs.

insights.claim: Perun notes international treaty bars weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit - nuclear, biological, chemical or radiological battle stations - while purely kinetic weapons are a different story, with the Soviet Almaz and its 23-mm cannon being the one publicly known conventionally armed space station to have fired in orbit.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The legal gap around kinetic orbital weapons is the opening any space-strike program would exploit - relevant to space-defence policy risk.

insights.claim: Perun cites RAND's 2002 'Space Weapons Earth Wars' study for the US Air Force as pitching four advantages for space-based weapons - access and reach, rapid response, difficulty of attack for states without ASAT capability, and difficulty of defence - with response times of minutes to hours matched only by long-range ballistic missiles.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The canonical justification set for orbital strike is two decades old and public - useful for anticipating how new space-weapons budgets will be argued.
insights.quote: space-based weapons could offer response times from several minutes to several hours. Only long-range ballistic missiles can achieve similar performance.

insights.claim: Perun relays RAND's physics constraint that long, slender, heavy, non-explosive penetrators are useful only against targets vulnerable to vertical penetration - tall buildings, missile silos, ships and hardened aircraft shelters - and not against runways, deeply buried bunkers, bridges or low, long buildings.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Rod-from-God target sets are far narrower than popular perception, which caps the real military value of any such program.
insights.quote: Suitable weapons would include tall buildings, missile silos, ships, and hardened aircraft shelters, but not runways, deeply buried bunkers, bridges, and low, long buildings.

insights.claim: Perun gives RAND's sizing example of a roughly 1 m, 100 kg rod penetrating about 1.5 m of steel, versus other studies contemplating 100-plus-ton rods, and notes global responsive coverage requires an estimated absentee ratio of about six satellites per one on station.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The absentee ratio is the hidden multiplier that makes orbital strike constellations economically brutal - the same logic applies to any responsive-coverage space architecture.

insights.claim: Perun argues orbital kinetic strike is dominated on cost by terrestrial alternatives in 2026 - hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles like Russia's RS-24 or China's DF-21 and hypersonic glide vehicles like the DF-17 or America's Dark Eagle - so the only way to justify the space option is to write a genuinely global, deny-sanctuary requirement that long range alone cannot satisfy.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expanding hypersonic and ballistic inventories keep crowding out orbital strike on cost-per-effect - a reason to discount space-strike program hype.

insights.claim: Perun cites RAND's judgement that kinetic energy weapons hold little interest for the United States, which already has effective weapons against that target class, but could be desirable for countries seeking global power projection without duplicating the US investment in terrestrial forces - a shortcut argument for middle powers.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Aspirant powers, not the US, are the plausible customers for exotic global-strike concepts - relevant to proliferation and export-control risk.
insights.quote: kinetic energy weapons could be desirable for countries that seek global power projection without having to duplicate the US investment in terrestrial forces.

insights.claim: Perun points to collapsing launch costs as the one variable that has genuinely improved the orbital-strike case since 2003, citing a recent US contract for another 18 Falcon 9 launches over 14 months for about 1.6 billion US dollars while cautioning those numbers do not transfer to lifting classified heavy payloads.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Commercial launch pricing is the key input that makes previously absurd space architectures financially arguable - a structural tailwind for launch providers.

insights.claim: Perun argues an orbital rod system's real return may be psychological rather than military, noting many weapons across history commanded more public fear than their raw capabilities merited, so the marginal spend might be better placed on media presence than on more satellites and rods.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Perceived capability can substitute for real capability in deterrence - a reason to discount headline weapons announcements as signalling rather than capability.
insights.quote: you can name plenty of weapon systems across history that have commanded more public attention, more fear, and more apprehension than their actual raw capabilities merited

insights.claim: Perun flags that an orbital kinetic system creates first-strike instability for its owner because it is expensive, hard to intercept and low-signature on release - unlike a ballistic launch's thermal signature - yet is itself massively vulnerable to anti-satellite launchers, encouraging shoot-first postures.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Use-it-or-lose-it space assets are strategically destabilising, which is a policy and escalation risk factor for space-weapons investment.

themes.theme: Dual-Use Space Programs as Budget Arbitrage

insights.claim: Perun cites the head of US Space Command stating in 2025 that the country needs space fires and space weapon systems, positioning space weaponisation as an openly stated official requirement rather than a hypothetical.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Explicit senior-officer demand signals precede budget lines - a leading indicator for space-defence contracting.
insights.quote: we need space fires and we need space weapon systems

insights.claim: Perun quantifies lunar base ambition as out of reach for a single middle power by noting NASA's plan calls for more than 80 launches to the moon and delivery of north of 210 tons of cargo.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Lunar infrastructure economics force coalition or commercial participation - single-nation lunar programs are not credible at that cargo scale.

insights.claim: Perun's general management lesson for pet projects with big budgets is to technically deliver exactly what you are told to do while generating as many genuinely useful outcomes as possible on the side - illustrated by building an astronaut selection, training, launch, landing, rover and habitat capability under the cover of a space marine program.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Dual-use structuring is how exotic mandates get converted into durable industrial capability - and how to read seemingly absurd defence line items.
insights.quote: You find a way to technically deliver exactly what you're being told to do while on the side making sure you generate as many actually useful outcomes as possible.

insights.claim: Perun argues the hard part of a military space program is space itself, not the weapons - noting Soviet-era studies envisaged very light, simple small arms for lunar infantry use and the Almaz gun was relatively simple - so a weapons mandate can fund the expensive general-purpose capability and be dropped cheaply later.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Military space budgets reliably subsidise civilian-usable launch, habitat and crew capability - the same R&D-spillover pattern seen historically.
insights.quote: it's not so much that weaponizing space is hard, it's just that space is hard

insights.claim: Perun endorses cheap resilience measures that a modern EW-saturated, signature-conscious battlefield rewards, specifically burying power and fibre optic cable to prepared defensive positions in a pre-war period to sustain infantry and guarantee connectivity for forward-deployed UAS and UGVs, plus balloons and zeppelins as cheap airborne sensor and drone-relay platforms.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Fibre, buried power and cheap high-altitude platforms are low-cost, high-leverage counter-EW investments already validated in Ukraine.

insights.claim: Perun closes on the honest verdict that the crowdsourced package would be a genuinely bad investment and that outsourcing a major procurement to the internet is inadvisable, while noting many non-Patreon submissions were serious alternative force designs rather than deliberate sabotage.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Frames the whole episode as a deliberate thought experiment - treat the specific buys as illustrative, and the requirements-and-opportunity-cost lessons as the transferable content.
insights.quote: Would it be a good investment? No, but it would be an investment.
